title: Blog 1
content:
Designing a cost-optimised IoT data flow (MQTT → AWS IoT Core → Glue → S3) for small projects Author: Ngo Thi Kim Ngan (team member) · Team blog, shared under the FCAJ rules
Post: AWS Study Group VN
The post lives in the AWS Study Group VN group, so only group members can open it. Below is my own summary of it.
The problem A sensor system that sends a small JSON message over MQTT every few seconds produces millions of files in Amazon S3 after a few months. The post estimates that 10 devices sending every 10 seconds for 3 months create about 7.7 million files. At that point PUT/GET request charges can exceed storage charges, and Amazon Athena has to open every JSON file, so queries become slow and expensive to scan.
Proposed architecture The data flow has two stages and no servers:
Raw collection: the AWS IoT Core Rule Engine filters messages with SQL and writes them straight to a raw S3 bucket, partitioned by year=/month=/day=/hour=. No EC2 instance or Lambda function is needed just to receive MQTT. Compaction: once a day, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler starts an AWS Glue job that reads the previous day’s JSON, cleans the data types, merges the files and writes Apache Parquet (Snappy compression) to a curated bucket. Cleanup: an S3 Lifecycle rule deletes raw JSON after 7 days, which keeps a week of raw data for debugging without paying to store it forever. Results reported in the post For a scenario of 10 million messages per month (about 2 GB of raw JSON):
Metric Before After Storage in S3 ~2.0 GB ~280 MB Number of files in S3 ~10,000,000 ~30 (1 file/day) Data scanned by Athena for a one-column query ~2.0 GB ~40 MB The post also suggests how to keep Glue cheap: with Spark, use the G.1X worker type and at most 2 workers; for data under a few hundred MB per day, use Glue Python Shell (0.0625 DPU) with the awswrangler library.
What I took away S3 cost is not only about storage size; the number of requests and objects also has to be counted at design time. A columnar format such as Parquet sharply reduces how much data Athena scans, which directly lowers query cost. Using built-in service features (IoT rules, S3 Lifecycle) instead of custom code leaves fewer components to operate.

title: Overview and Architecture
content:
The problem Scam messages targeting older adults often look exactly like genuine ones: fake banks, fake police, fake “traffic camera fines”, or “your child is in the emergency room, transfer money now”. What they have in common is that they push the recipient to act immediately, before they have a chance to ask anyone. Ask First creates a place to ask first: the user forwards the content to the bot, and the bot replies within seconds.
The accompanying technical challenges:
Users also send screenshots, so the system must be able to read Vietnamese text in images. The content contains phone numbers, account numbers, and OTP codes. Raw images must never leave our own infrastructure; only text with the numbers masked may be sent to the LLM. Traffic is low and irregular (a few hundred to a few thousand checks per month), so paying for a server running 24/7 is not an option. Solution on AWS The system is split into two parts:
Ingestion and orchestration (Java 21, 3 Lambda functions): receives updates from Telegram, batches messages sent in quick succession, enqueues jobs, and sends results back to the user and their trusted contacts. Analysis (Python 3.12, 1 Lambda container image): reads text in images, masks personal information, runs the rule set, searches a knowledge base of scam scenarios, and only then asks an LLM on Amazon Bedrock if the rules are not confident enough. Architecture diagram The journey of a screenshot The diagram has 17 numbered arrows. I group them into 5 stages following the path of one image:
Stage Arrows What happens Components A. Receive 1–3 The user sends an image. Telegram POSTs the update to the webhook Function URL. Requests without the correct X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header are rejected with 401. webhook writes the message to the BUFFER#<chat> buffer in DynamoDB. Lambda webhook, DynamoDB B. Enqueue 4–5 webhook replies “⏳” to the user, pushes an AnalyzeJob to SQS with a 3-second delay (to batch messages sent in quick succession), then returns HTTP 200 to Telegram. worker picks up the job. SQS jobs, Lambda worker C. Analyze 6–12 worker invokes ai (alias live), sending only the file_id, not the image. ai downloads the image into memory itself using the bot token read from SSM, uses models loaded from S3 to run OCR, masks PII, runs the rules, probes shortened links, queries RAG, checks for prompt attacks with Guardrails, and then asks Bedrock. The verdict is cached for 24 hours in DynamoDB. Lambda ai, S3, SSM, DynamoDB, Bedrock D. Reply 13–17 worker edits the “⏳” message into the result, notifies trusted contacts if the risk is high, stores a CHECK# record (metadata only, 30-day TTL), and may schedule a follow-up question 15 minutes later. Lambda worker, Telegram E. On failure (dashed line) A job that fails 5 times goes to the DLQ. worker-dlq tells the user the bot is busy, and the CloudWatch alarm transitions to ALARM and sends an email through SNS. SQS DLQ, worker-dlq, CloudWatch, SNS In the team’s shared environment, Bedrock lives in a different account (AI1’s account), so ai must call sts:AssumeRole into that account before calling Bedrock (arrow 11). When you follow this workshop in a single account, just enable the Bedrock models in your own account and skip the assume role step.
AWS services and why they were chosen Service Used for Why chosen, and what was considered AWS Lambda (Java 21 zip) webhook, worker, worker-dlq Pay per invocation; Function URLs provide an HTTPS endpoint out of the box, so no API Gateway is needed. AWS Lambda (container image) ai The OCR libraries and ONNX Runtime exceed the 250 MB limit of a zip package; images allow up to 10 GB. Runs on CPU, no GPU required. Amazon ECR Stores the ai image Lambda container images can only be pulled from ECR. Amazon S3 Models (OCR 32 MB, VietOCR 90 MB, embedder 123 MB) and the knowledge base index (0.3 MB) Swapping a model does not require rebuilding the image; files are versioned by prefix, so rolling back is easy. Amazon SQS + DLQ Buffer between the ingestion part and the analysis part Telegram receives HTTP 200 in under 1 second even though analysis takes several seconds; retries, the 3-second delay for batching messages, and moving failed jobs to the DLQ are all built-in SQS features. Amazon DynamoDB A single table for users, consent, message buffers, results, and cache On-demand, TTL automatically deletes old data, zero cost when nobody is using it. Amazon Bedrock + Guardrails LLM judge (Qwen3 32B, with gpt-oss-120b as fallback) and prompt attack blocking Pay per token, low-cost open-weight models; no need to operate GPUs ourselves. SSM Parameter Store Bot token, webhook secret (SecureString), stack configuration Secrets are kept out of code and out of Lambda environment variables. CloudWatch + SNS JSON logs, metrics, DLQ alarm sending email Available for every Lambda function, no agent to install. AWS SAM / CloudFormation Infrastructure as code (infra/template.yaml) One command to build + deploy; the entire stack can be recreated. IAM A dedicated role per Lambda function, least privilege For example, the ai role can only read the model bucket and a single SSM parameter. Not used: VPC and NAT Gateway (a NAT Gateway alone costs about 32 USD/month even with zero messages), API Gateway, Step Functions, EC2/SageMaker with GPUs.
Mapping to AWS Well-Architected Each pillar comes with a piece of evidence I verified on the live environment (details in the following sections).
Pillar Design Verified evidence Operational Excellence Backend stack in SAM; ai image tagged by commit; the ai Lambda has versions + a live alias so a rollback is one command. The live alias has gone through 11 versions, each with the commit in its description (5.5). Security Function URL rejects requests missing the secret; secrets in SSM SecureString; least-privilege roles; S3 blocks public access; PII is masked before reaching Bedrock; logs contain no message content. A POST without the secret returns 401 (5.6); scanning CloudWatch logs found no message content or tokens (5.7). Reliability SQS retries + DLQ, worker-dlq sends a busy notice, verdict cache, “rules only” mode when the LLM fails, RapidOCR results are still returned if VietOCR fails. Blocking ai with reserved concurrency 0: the job was tried 5 times, went to the DLQ, and the user received exactly one “busy” message (5.7). Performance Efficiency ai at 3008 MB (about 1.7 vCPU); models preloaded during the INIT phase; small models running on CPU (ONNX). Measured 3 memory settings: 1769 MB hit the 10-second INIT limit, 3008 MB had a 6.2-second INIT (5.7). Cost Optimization No hourly-billed components; DynamoDB on-demand; LLM skipped when the rules are already confident. Actual cost for the whole account from 1–26/11/2026: about 0.10 USD before credits (5.9). Sustainability No machine is kept running while waiting for work; when the bot is idle, compute drops to zero as well. Not scored in FCAJ; included to complete the checklist.

title: AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 (Watch Party)
content:
AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026: Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party Item Details Date Tuesday, 29/09/2026 Venue AWS office, 26th floor, Bitexco Tower, Ho Chi Minh City (live stream from the main stage in Hanoi) Overall theme Agentic AI Speakers AWS leaders and AWS customers (live keynote) My role Attendee Programme Live keynote: customers describing how they use Agentic AI to modernise and scale their systems. Selected technical sessions from the “Builders x AI” track. On-site networking with engineers and tech practitioners in Ho Chi Minh City. What I took away I watched the event with one question in mind: when should AI decide, and when should code decide? What I noted:
Retrieve first, generate second. Many customer stories fed internal data in before calling the model, instead of relying on what the model remembers. That is RAG. Every step must be measurable. With a multi-step system, you need to know which step went wrong, not just that the final answer is wrong. Cost follows each call. An AI feature that is cheap in a trial can become expensive in production if the number of model calls is not estimated up front. Connection to my work RAG. Six weeks later I built the local RAG for Ask First: a corpus of 103 scam warnings, an int8 e5-small embedder and a retriever (PR #147), then wired it into the real pipeline with scenario-based citations (PR #151). Running the embedder inside Lambda means the team does not pay for a separate vector service. Measuring each step. The “every step must be measurable” idea is why I built separate measurements: PII masking on 500 samples (PR #158), the OTP rule (PR #159), and an eval gate that runs on every PR (PR #153). Cost. In my OCR blog I converted VietOCR’s extra latency into GB-seconds and USD per 1,000 images instead of just saying “a bit slower”. Lesson A trustworthy AI system does not come from the biggest model, but from every step having a measurement and a clear limit.

title: Blog 2
content:
Testing a serverless, event-driven flow (SQS + DLQ + DynamoDB) locally with LocalStack and Java 21 Author: Ngo Thi Kim Ngan (team member) · Team blog, shared under the FCAJ rules
Post: AWS Study Group VN
The post lives in the AWS Study Group VN group, so only group members can open it. Below is my own summary of it.
Context The asynchronous flow in the post is: an event goes into Amazon SQS, an AWS Lambda function (Java 21) processes it, writes to Amazon DynamoDB and reads configuration from SSM Parameter Store, with a DLQ for failed messages. Deploying to AWS to try every small fix is slow and can cause unexpected charges.
The “local-first” approach Emulate the services locally: LocalStack runs SQS, the DLQ, DynamoDB and SSM on the developer’s machine. Keep the endpoint switch clean: with the AWS SDK for Java v2, endpointOverride(URI.create(localEndpoint)) is called only in local mode (http://localhost:4566); in the cloud the default endpoint is used, so the same code runs in both places. Test both the happy path and the failure path: send a valid payload to check that the item lands in DynamoDB and the message is deleted from the main queue; send a bad payload to check that the message ends up in the DLQ after the configured number of retries. Go to the cloud last: build and deploy with AWS SAM only once the logic and configuration work locally. What I took away The failure path (retries, DLQ) should be tested on purpose like the main path, because it is the hardest part to observe once it runs on AWS. Keeping the endpoint choice in one place stops the code from branching all over between local and cloud. Our Ask First project also uses SQS with a DLQ for background processing, so the DLQ test approach in the post applies directly.

title: Preparing the Account and Tools
content:
This section is done once. It takes about 45 minutes, mostly for installing tools.
Step 1: Secure the account before creating resources Enable MFA on the root account, and stop using root for day-to-day work. Create a dedicated IAM user for deployment (I use the user ai2-dev). The workshop needs permissions to create CloudFormation stacks, Lambda, IAM roles, DynamoDB, SQS, S3, ECR, SSM, CloudWatch, SNS, and to call Bedrock. In a learning account, the quickest approach is to add the user to a group with AdministratorAccess; in a shared account, restrict permissions to the services listed above. Create AWS Budgets to receive an email when spending exceeds a threshold. I set a budget of 50 USD/month with alerts at 80% and 100%. Step 2: Enable Amazon Bedrock models in Sydney The ai Lambda runs in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) but calls Bedrock in Sydney (ap-southeast-2), because when the team chose the models, Sydney offered the open-weight models while Singapore did not yet. The two models required:
Role Model ID Primary evaluator (judge) qwen.qwen3-32b-v1:0 Fallback when the judge fails openai.gpt-oss-120b-1:0 Verify directly with the CLI rather than only looking at the console. The command below sends a short prompt to Qwen3 32B:
aws bedrock-runtime converse --region ap-southeast-2 ` --model-id qwen.qwen3-32b-v1:0 ` --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Trả lời 1 từ: xin chào"}]}]' ` --inference-config maxTokens=20 ` --query "output.message.content[0].text" --output text Result on my account (27/11/2026):
Chào If you get an AccessDeniedException, open Amazon Bedrock → Model access in the ap-southeast-2 Region and request access to the two models above.
Step 3: Install the tools The versions below are the ones I used when writing the workshop; newer versions also work.
Tool Version used Used for AWS CLI v2 2.41.1 All AWS commands AWS SAM CLI 1.173.0 Building and deploying the backend stack Java (Temurin JDK) 21.0.13 Building the 3 Java Lambda functions Docker Desktop 29.5.3 Building the ai Lambda image Python + uv Python 3.13, uv 0.12.5 Running the AI scripts (downloading models, uploading to S3, testing) Git 2.45 Fetching the source code SAM requires the mvn command, but the repo only ships the Maven Wrapper (mvnw.cmd). If Maven is not installed, sam build reports that mvn cannot be found. My workaround: create an mvn.cmd file that points to the repo’s wrapper and put that folder at the front of PATH (see 5.4, step 3). sam build must be run in PowerShell; Git Bash cannot pass this shim through to SAM.
Step 4: Configure the AWS CLI with a named profile aws configure --profile ai2test # enter the IAM user's access key, region ap-southeast-1 $env:AWS_PROFILE = "ai2test" # only applies to this PowerShell window $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" aws sts get-caller-identity The result must be the IAM user you just created, not root:
{ "UserId": "AIDA...", "Account": "<ACCOUNT_ID>", "Arn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:user/ai2-dev" } Step 5: Get the source code git clone https://github.com/ask-first-fcaj/ask-first.git cd ask-first git switch main Folders used in the workshop:
Folder Contents infra/ template.yaml (SAM), samconfig.toml backend/ScamProtection/ Java code for webhook, worker, worker-dlq and the shared common module ai/ Python code for the ai Lambda, Dockerfile, config/artifacts.yaml, scripts in ai/scripts/ kb/, prompts/ Knowledge base of scam scenarios and LLM prompts, packaged into the image scripts/ set_webhook.py, set_commands.py for Telegram contracts/fixtures/ Sample requests for test-invoking the ai Lambda Step 6: Create the Telegram bot In Telegram, open @BotFather → send /newbot → set a display name and a username (must end with bot). BotFather returns a token in the form 123456789:AA....
The token is the key that controls the bot. I once leaked the token in a screenshot sent to the team and had to /revoke it to get a new one. Since then: redact the token line before taking a screenshot, and store the token only in SSM (5.4, step 1), never in a .env file in the repo or in the command history.

title: Proposal
content:
Project Proposal: Ask First (Hỏi Trước) Author: Võ Hoàng Quốc Minh, AI2 member of the team. This proposal presents our team project from the angle of the parts I was responsible for: the AI pipeline running locally inside Lambda, the measurement and evaluation data, and the shared AWS environment of the team.
1. Problem and solution overview The problem in one sentence: an elderly person receives a message about a “traffic fine”, an “insurance refund” or a “police summons” and needs someone to tell them whether to act on it, before they tap the link or read out an OTP code.
The solution: a Telegram bot called Hỏi Trước (“Ask First”). Users forward a message, paste a link or send a screenshot. The bot replies with a short Vietnamese verdict: a risk level, reasons grounded in the wording of the message itself, what to do next, and related official warnings. If the user has consented to link a relative, that relative is notified when the message is high risk.
Three points shape the design, and they are also the three areas I worked on most:
Most of the “understanding” runs locally inside Lambda, with no per-token cost: reading text from images (OCR), masking personal data, rule-based scoring, URL analysis, and retrieving related warnings (RAG). Only the final classification step calls an open-weight LLM on Amazon Bedrock, and only with masked text. Every AI change must be backed by measurements: each component has a dataset, a re-runnable measurement script and a clear pass threshold; evaluation runs in CI to block PRs that lower quality. Everything runs serverless on AWS, with no always-on servers and no VPC/NAT; cost follows the number of checks. Item Details Channel Telegram Bot API, webhook Team 4 people: BE1, BE2 (Java 21), AI1, AI2 (Python 3.12) Timeframe 6 weeks, 19/10/2026 – 29/11/2026 Region Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, S3 in ap-southeast-1; Bedrock in ap-southeast-2 Source code ask-first-fcaj/ask-first 2. Problem statement Scam messages are written to make the reader act immediately. A fake message usually has three parts: a worrying reason (unpaid bills, a traffic fine, a relative in trouble), time pressure (“within 24 hours”), and a harmful action (tap a link, install an app, read out an OTP, transfer money). By the time the reader performs the third part, it is usually too late.
Elderly people find it hard to check by themselves. They struggle to tell a real domain from a look-alike, rarely know a bank’s official hotline, and often receive these messages when no family member is around. Banks mostly intervene at the transfer step, which is after the scammer has already done the persuading.
Three technical problems I had to solve in the AI part:
Problem Why it is hard How the project handles it Most scams arrive as screenshots Images contain accented Vietnamese; URLs wrap across lines or lose their first characters Local OCR, regex-based URL repair, re-reading Vietnamese lines with VietOCR Messages contain the user’s phone number, bank account, ID number, OTP Personal data must not leave Lambda Mask PII into tokens ([SĐT_1], [OTP_1]) before any Bedrock call The LLM may hallucinate, be slow, or fail The bot must never go silent or give a misleading answer A rule layer independent of the LLM with a score floor; RAG retrieves real warnings to cite 3. Objectives and scope The overall goal is an MVP running for real on AWS, ready for the demo on 27/11/2026 and the workshop submission on 29/11/2026.
Measurable success criteria (thresholds set up front in docs/system-architecture.md §1.3 and the gates in docs/implementation-plan.md §4):
Area Metric Pass threshold Measured with Classification quality Recall on scam messages ≥ 90% eval/run_eval.py, enforced in CI Classification quality False alarms on benign-but-suspicious messages ≤ 10% same OCR (gate G2) Correct URL transcription on an independent image set ≥ 90% eval/ocr_benchmark.py OCR (gate G2) CER ≤ 10% same RAG (milestone M3) Scenario card Recall@4 on real_scam ≥ 90% RAG eval RAG (milestone M3) Query time < 100 ms measured on Lambda Latency End-to-end p95 with a warm container, text and images ≤ 15 seconds CloudWatch, latency_ms logs Cost Per check ≤ 0.005 USD actual token counts Privacy Eval samples leaking numbers or OTPs into the prompt 0 security tests for mask() In MVP scope:
Inputs: text, forwarded messages, links, screenshots and albums; consecutive messages are batched. AI pipeline: normalization, OCR, PII masking, rules, URL analysis (including SSRF-safe expansion of short links), RAG, Guardrails, LLM judge, fusion, template-based replies. Users: explicit consent, consent withdrawal, data deletion, linking and alerting relatives, management through chat commands. Operations: kill switch to fall back to rules-only mode, DLQ alarm, budgets. Out of scope for the 6 weeks (postponed in plan v3): voice/ASR, VLM for hard images, multi-turn follow-up questions, Telegram Mini App, Phase 2 (living knowledge base), pilot with households outside the team.
My share of this scope: the image set and OCR spike (AI-20), PII masking (AI-22), normalization and rules (AI-23), URL intel (AI-24a, wiring url_net in AI-24b), knowledge base and validator (AI-25), Telegram media download and S3ArtifactStore (AI-03b), local RAG (AI-29, INT-03), eval in CI (AI-09), VietOCR re-reading of Vietnamese (AI-26), wiring PIPELINE_IMPL=real to S3, DynamoDB and Telegram (INT-01), and building the team’s shared AWS environment.
4. Solution architecture The team’s shared diagram, showing only the MVP that is running.
4.1 Three Lambdas, three responsibilities webhook (Java): receives updates, checks secret_token, deduplicates, batches messages, returns 200 to Telegram quickly and pushes a job to SQS. worker (Java): reads the job, invokes ai, sends the verdict, alerts relatives, writes metadata. ai (Python, 3008 MB container image): the whole AI pipeline. This is the part I wrote and operated the most. The Java ↔ Python boundary is a JSON Schema contract (gate G0). Thanks to it, the AI side could be developed and measured entirely in Python without waiting for the backend.
4.2 The AI pipeline inside the ai Lambda Step Runs where What it does Key measurement (source) Media download ai Lambda Fetches the image from Telegram by file_id, kept only in memory and /tmp; images never pass through the Java payload AI-03b OCR Local, ONNX RapidOCR (PP-OCRv6 small) detects lines and reads URLs/phone numbers; VietOCR re-reads accented lines; regex repairs URL prefixes Independent 16-image set: URLs 17/18 (94%), CER 7.2% (ocr-spike); correctly accented words 37% → 89% with VietOCR (ocr-vietocr) PII masking Local, regex + keywords Phone, bank account, ID number, OTP, email, numbers written in words → tokens Held-out: 130/132 PII items masked (mask-pii) Rules Local, rules.yaml Signals such as OTP requests, urgency, impersonating authorities; a score floor independent of the LLM OTP rules catch 100/100 scams, 1/100 false alarm on genuine messages (otp-rules) URL intel Local + controlled network Extracts domains, detects brand look-alikes, expands short links via SSRF-safe url_net AI-24a, AI-24b (PR #175) RAG Local, e5-small int8 Finds the closest scenario cards and .gov.vn warnings by in-memory cosine similarity Dev machine: Recall@4 35/38 = 92.1%; on Lambda: p95 45 ms (lambda-p95) Guard + Judge Bedrock (Sydney) Guardrails PROMPT_ATTACK, then Qwen3 32B returns structured JSON; gpt-oss-120b as fallback Text p95 3.5 s with a warm container Fuse + Respond Local Combines rule and LLM scores into 4 levels, replies from templates, never lets the LLM write freely No message over 600 characters (readability) OCR and RAG models are preloaded in the Lambda INIT phase (PR #173), so the first request after a cold start does not wait for model loading. Weights live on S3 with checksums; swapping a model does not require rebuilding the image.

A Function URL is enough for the webhook, so no API Gateway Lambda container image + Amazon ECR Packaging onnxruntime, RapidOCR, VietOCR, the embedder Zip packages are capped at 250 MB, too small for ML libraries; images go up to 10 GB, the team set its own 2 GB cap Amazon SQS + DLQ webhook → worker queue, batching via DelaySeconds Decouples the Telegram reply from slow processing; built-in retries; the DLQ keeps failed jobs for manual handling Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) Users, consent, relatives, check metadata, CACHE# and URL# caches, FLAGS Key-based access, TTL for automatic deletion, no capacity management Amazon S3 OCR/embedding weights, the RAG index, donated samples auto-deleted after 30 days Cheap, versions and checksums for artifacts Amazon Bedrock + Guardrails LLM judge and prompt injection filtering Open-weight models priced per token, no GPU operations. On 24/11/2026 the team agreed to use this account as the shared runtime environment. Bedrock stays in AI1’s account, and the ai Lambda reaches it through a role (BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN).

title: Blog 3
content:
Lambda and EventBridge: using an event-driven architecture to refresh data every day Author: Tri Duc Vo (team member) · Team blog, shared under the FCAJ rules
Post: AWS Study Group VN
The post lives in the AWS Study Group VN group, so only group members can open it. Below is my own summary of it.
The problem The author wanted a single web page that shows fuel prices, gold prices, esports scores and the weather, instead of opening several tabs every morning. The requirements: no server running 24/7, each data source refreshed at its own pace, one failing source must not break the whole page, new sources easy to add, and a small personal budget.
Architecture EventBridge Scheduler (one schedule per source, payload {"source": ...}) → Lambda Collector → S3 data/<source>.json → S3 "Object Created" → EventBridge Rule (filters prefix data/) → Lambda Renderer → S3 index.html → CloudFront (invalidation) EventBridge Scheduler is the system’s clock: each source has its own schedule (weather every 3 hours, scores every 30 minutes, fuel and gold daily or weekly), set in Vietnam’s time zone, with retries and a DLQ for failed invocations. Lambda Collector is shared by all sources: it reads the source name from the payload, calls the API, normalises the result into compact JSON and writes it to S3. If a source fails, it reports the error and does not overwrite the old file, so the page keeps the previous data. EventBridge Rule catches new files under data/ and invokes Lambda Renderer, which merges the data, rebuilds index.html and refreshes the CloudFront cache. Two pitfalls called out in the post Filter on the data/ prefix. The renderer writes index.html to the same bucket; if the rule matched every new object, index.html itself would trigger the renderer again and create an infinite loop. S3 delivers events at least once, so duplicates can happen. The renderer is idempotent: it always rebuilds the page from the current data and overwrites it, so running it again does not change the result. What I took away Splitting the system by events lets each part run, fail and change independently; adding a source only needs one more schedule and one more normaliser. When a function reads from and writes to the same bucket, the risk of it triggering itself has to be considered right away. Showing an update timestamp (updatedAt) for each section is a simple way to tell readers which data is stale.

title: Uploading AI Models to S3
content:
The ai Lambda uses four sets of model files. They are not inside the container image; they live on S3. When the Lambda starts, it downloads the files to /tmp/artifacts and verifies their SHA-256 before loading them.
Why separate the models from the image:
The image is about 250 MB lighter, so builds and pushes are faster. Swapping a model (for example, a new knowledge base index) only requires uploading to S3 and changing one line of configuration, without rebuilding the image. Each model version lives under a versioned prefix, so rolling back only requires pointing the configuration to the old prefix. The four artifacts and where they are defined The single source of truth is ai/config/artifacts.yaml: the name, version, S3 prefix, and SHA-256 of every file.
Artifact S3 prefix Contents Size ocr ocr/ppocrv6-small-rapidocr3.10.0/ RapidOCR: text detection, recognition, and orientation models (ONNX fp32) 32 MB vietocr vietocr/vgg-seq2seq-0.3.13-fp32/ VietOCR exported to ONNX: re-reads Vietnamese lines where RapidOCR drops characters 90 MB embedder embedder/e5-small-qint8-614241f/ int8 multilingual-e5-small for generating RAG vectors 123 MB kb_index kb_index/kb-2026.11.11/ Vectors for the 21 scenario cards + 103 warning articles in kb/ 0.3 MB Step 1: Create the model bucket $env:AWS_PROFILE = "ai2test"; $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $acct = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text $bucket = "askfirst-ai2-test-$acct" # bucket names are globally unique, so append the account ID aws s3 mb "s3://$bucket" aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket $bucket A newly created bucket has all 4 Block Public Access flags enabled; the last command must print all 4 values as true.
Step 2: Download and build the files Run in the ai/ folder. The fetch_* scripts stop automatically if the SHA-256 of a downloaded file differs from artifacts.yaml.
cd ai uv run python scripts/fetch_ocr_models.py out/ocr uv run python scripts/fetch_embedder.py out/embedder uv run python scripts/build_index.py out/embedder out/kb_index --version kb-2026.11.11 At the end of the run, build_index.py prints the hashes of the two index files. The vectors are floating-point numbers, so running on a different machine may produce differences in the last digit and therefore a different hash. If that happens, copy your hash into the kb_index entry of artifacts.yaml before the image build step in 5.5, because this configuration file is packaged into the image.
VietOCR needs PyTorch for the ONNX export, so use a separate Python environment, isolated from the Lambda environment. How to set up that environment is described at the top of ai/scripts/export_vietocr_onnx.py; then:
.venv-vietocr\Scripts\python scripts/export_vietocr_onnx.py out/vietocr The script downloads the original weights, stops if the SHA-256 is wrong, and compares each part of the ONNX version against PyTorch (error ≤ 1e-4) before writing the files. Skipping VietOCR is also fine: OCR still runs with RapidOCR, it just reads diacritics poorly (see the lessons in 5.11).
Step 3: Upload with SHA-256 verification $env:ARTIFACT_BUCKET = $bucket uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py ocr out/ocr uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py vietocr out/vietocr uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py embedder out/embedder uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py kb_index out/kb_index The script verifies every file of an artifact first; if even one file mismatches, nothing is uploaded. Verify again:
aws s3 ls "s3://$bucket/" --recursive --summarize --human-readable Step 4: Test downloading the way the Lambda will Before having a Lambda, I ran the exact S3ArtifactStore class the Lambda uses, right on my machine:
uv run python -c "from pathlib import Path; from askfirst.artifacts.s3 import S3ArtifactStore as S; s=S('$bucket', Path('config/artifacts.yaml'), root=Path('out/dl')); [print(n, s.path(n)) for n in ('ocr','embedder','kb_index')]" Measured on 19/11/2026 (from a machine in Vietnam): ocr 2.4 seconds, embedder 5.9 seconds, kb_index 0.4 seconds. A second run downloads nothing because the files already exist with the correct SHA-256.
Negative test. I deliberately uploaded a meta.json that was off by 1 byte and called it again: the class raises ArtifactError: sai sha256 (“wrong sha256”) instead of loading the corrupted file. I then re-uploaded the correct file. This is why the Lambda never runs with a tampered or partially downloaded model.

title: Blog 4
content:
Vietnamese OCR on AWS Lambda: when the model reads “chuyển tiền” as “chuyn tin” Re-reading with a second model, merging word by word, running on Lambda with ONNX and S3
Author: Vo Hoang Quoc Minh (AI2, Ask First team)
I submitted this post to the AWS Study Group but it was not approved for publication, so there is no post link. The full text is kept here.
A screenshot contains the sentence “Quý khách vui lòng chuyển tiền vào tài khoản an toàn” (“Please transfer money to a safe account”). The OCR returns:
Quý khách vui lòng chuyn tin vào tài khon an toàn These are not lost diacritics. The model drops the vowels entirely. For a scam-detection bot, “chuyển tiền” (transfer money) is one of the most important phrases to catch.
This post describes how our team fixed that in the Ask First (Hỏi Trước) project, under one constraint: OCR must run inside AWS Lambda, with no GPU and without sending images to any outside service. Every number here was measured on the team’s 66 labelled images and on a real Lambda in ap-southeast-1.
1. Context: why OCR has to run inside Lambda Ask First is a Telegram bot that helps elderly people check suspicious messages, links and screenshots before acting on them. The user forwards the content to the bot, and the bot replies with a risk level in plain Vietnamese.
The AI part runs in a Python 3.12 Lambda packaged as a container image with 3008 MB of memory. The pipeline is: read text from the image (OCR) → mask personal data → rules layer → find the most similar scam scenario (RAG) → LLM on Amazon Bedrock → combine scores.
Design principle: raw images are only processed by models running locally inside Lambda. Only text with phone and account numbers masked leaves the Lambda. That is why OCR does not use an external service; it runs RapidOCR (PaddleOCR PP-OCRv6 models in ONNX format) directly on the Lambda CPU.
2. Symptom: losing diacritics is fine, losing letters is not The rules layer matches on text with diacritics removed. “chuyển tiền”, “chuyen tien” and “chuyền tiến” all become “chuyen tien” before comparison. We stripped every diacritic from the ground-truth text of the 66 images: not a single image changed its rule result. Losing diacritics is not the problem.
The problem is losing letters:
Correct text OCR output chuyển tiền (transfer money) chuyn tin tài khoản (account) tài khon số tiền (amount) s tin điểm (points) đim “chuyn tin” without diacritics is still “chuyn tin”, so the rule does not match. Across the 66 images, 15/33 rule signals were lost purely because of this. The share of accented words read correctly was 37% on the 50-image set and 27% on the 16-image set.
The cause sits inside the model file itself. The character dictionary of PP-OCRv6_rec_small (stored in the ONNX file metadata) has 18,708 characters. It includes á à ã â ă ê ô ơ ư đ but lacks 88 Vietnamese characters such as ả ạ ấ ộ ữ ự. With no character to emit, the model simply drops it. This is already reported on PaddleOCR’s GitHub (issue #18254).
3. Why not just replace the model The first idea everyone has: switch to another model.
The larger v6 model: same dictionary, same gaps. PP-OCRv5 latin: missing 99 characters, and worse at reading URLs. VietOCR alone (a Vietnamese-specific model): in our initial comparison, PaddleOCR detection + VietOCR recognition transcribed only 9/32 URLs correctly, versus 31/32 for RapidOCR. For an anti-scam bot, a URL with one wrong character breaks the whole domain check. So the question is not which model is better, but how to let each model do what it is good at:
RapidOCR: detect lines, read URLs, phone numbers and digits. VietOCR: read accented Vietnamese words. 4. Approach: selective re-reading, word-level merging How one image is processed:
Image | RapidOCR: detect lines + read each line | Line has at least 1 accented word and no URL? |-- no --> keep RapidOCR text |-- yes --> crop the line, VietOCR re-reads it | merge word by word with RapidOCR text | Final text --> mask PII --> rules layer --> ... Line filter. If RapidOCR already produced at least one accented word on a line, the line is almost certainly Vietnamese and may have lost letters. Lines containing a URL are not sent, because VietOCR often misreads URL endings. Across the 66 images, only 552 of 1,254 lines were sent for re-reading.
We tried removing the filter and sending every line: correct URLs on the 16-image set dropped from 17/18 to 10/18, phone numbers from 20/20 to 15/20. The filter is mandatory.
Merge per word, not per line. Our first version accepted or rejected whole lines and ran into two problems:
Lines mixing words and digits, such as “Gi chót đồi quà! 9082 đim”: VietOCR misread the digits, so the whole line had to be rejected, losing the correct words too. Scam messages that inject characters like “Ta,i,D’en’S;o’” to dodge filters: VietOCR reads something completely different, so those lines were rejected as well. The current version keeps the RapidOCR string and only replaces individual letter groups when VietOCR merely adds vowels:
Same consonant skeleton: “chuyn” and “chuyển” both have the skeleton c-h-y-n. VietOCR only adds vowels; it never removes them or changes consonants. Same upper/lower case pattern. Digits, punctuation, URLs and emails always keep the RapidOCR version. Result for the line above:
RapidOCR: Gi chót đồi quà! 9082 đim After merge: Giờ chót đồi quà! 9082 điểm (“đồi” still has the wrong tone mark because RapidOCR’s dictionary has ồ but not ổ. The rules layer strips diacritics before matching, so this has no effect.)
Cases that are not merged: VietOCR reading “+84 79 9165198” as “48479 91651980” (digits keep the RapidOCR version), and “BanK” as “Bank” (a case change, rejected).
Moving from line-level to word-level merging raised the share of correct accented words from 82% to 89% (50 images) and from 51% to 97% (16 images). The 16-image set contains many character-injected messages, so it improved the most.
5. Shipping to Lambda: four decisions a) Run with ONNX Runtime, keep PyTorch out of the image The original VietOCR is written in PyTorch. We exported it to ONNX as 3 files: cnn.onnx (79 MB), encoder.onnx and decoder.onnx, about 88 MB in total. Lambda only needs onnxruntime, numpy and Pillow, which RapidOCR already uses. No new dependency, and the image does not grow by hundreds of MB for PyTorch.
Decoding runs step by step in a Python loop. Precomputing the attention part that depends only on the encoder (once per line instead of once per step) made it about 2.7 times faster over 1,254 lines (measured on a dev machine), with identical output text.
b) Models live on S3, not inside the image Model files are uploaded to S3 under a versioned prefix (vietocr/vgg-seq2seq-0.3.13-fp32/). A config file in the repo records the version, prefix and the sha256 of each file. On startup, Lambda downloads them to /tmp and verifies sha256 before loading. To disable VietOCR, remove the version from the config file; no code change needed. To change the model, change the version; the old one stays on S3 for rollback.
c) Preload during the INIT phase Lambda has an INIT phase that runs once when a new execution environment is created, before the first request. We preload OCR and VietOCR there (running a small blank image through them). Otherwise the first user of every container waits longer: loading VietOCR alone adds about 1.1 seconds.
d) If loading fails, try only once If the files are not on S3 yet (for example, code deployed before the model was uploaded), the first load fails. OCR then still returns the RapidOCR text, logs one warning line, and that container skips re-reading until Lambda replaces it. No S3 call per image, and no failed request because of an auxiliary step.
6. Measuring on a real Lambda Every decision above was re-checked on a real Lambda, not just on a laptop. The method: package the 66 images into a temporary image together with production code and models, deploy it as a separate 3008 MB function, invoke it twice (the second run on a warm container), compare output with the dev machine, then delete the function and the image tag. The whole run takes a few minutes.
This is how we picked the right model variant. The int8 version (smaller and faster) did well on a laptop but clearly worse on Lambda’s CPU, so we chose fp32. With fp32, the output on Lambda matched the dev machine on all 66/66 images. The latency numbers in this post are also Lambda measurements, not CI-machine numbers.
7. Results The 50-image set is for development and the 16-image set is for testing. All images are synthetic or redacted; none contain real personal data.
Metric RapidOCR only + VietOCR Correct URLs (50 · 16 images) 31/32 · 17/18 31/32 · 17/18 Correct phone numbers 16/16 · 20/20 16/16 · 20/20 Correct accented words, 50 images 37% 89% Correct accented words, 16 images 27% 97% CER (50 · 16 images) 12.8% · 7.1% 6.8% · 5.3% Lost rule signals 15/33 6/33 URLs and phone numbers are unchanged, exactly what the filter was meant to protect. Lost rule signals dropped by more than half; the remainder mostly comes from other causes such as phrases split across two lines or lines containing URLs.
8. Trade-offs: latency and cost On a 3008 MB Lambda, re-reading adds p50 0.56 seconds per image. Images with many Vietnamese lines add more, since VietOCR reads line by line.
On cost, Lambda bills per GB-second. The x86 price in Singapore is 0.0000166667 USD/GB-second (AWS Price List API, first tier). With 3008 MB (about 2.94 GB):
0.56 extra seconds ≈ 1.65 GB-seconds ≈ 0.000027 USD per image 1,000 images ≈ 0.03 USD The cost is negligible compared with catching the right scam phrases.
Next optimisation directions:
More memory. Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory: about 1,769 MB equals 1 vCPU, up to 10,240 MB with 6 vCPUs. 3008 MB currently gives 2 vCPUs. More vCPUs can shorten run time, so total cost may not increase. Read several lines in parallel to use those vCPUs. Try arm64 Lambda (Graviton), cheaper than x86 per GB-second. Add new image sets to keep validating accuracy. Conclusion Three takeaways from our team:
Diagnose the symptom correctly before fixing. “Lost diacritics” and “lost letters” look alike but have very different impact. One small test (stripping all diacritics from the ground truth) pointed straight at the real failure. You do not need a perfect model. Two models, each doing what it does best, plus a strict enough merge rule, beat replacing the model outright. Measure in the real environment. A temporary Lambda function, run for a few minutes and then deleted, gives trustworthy numbers for choosing models and configuration before deploying. References PaddleOCR issue #18254 (PP-OCRv6 missing Vietnamese characters) RapidOCR VietOCR AWS Lambda: Configure memory (memory and vCPU) AWS Lambda: Execution environment lifecycle (INIT phase) AWS Lambda: Container images AWS Lambda pricing ONNX Runtime quantization #AWS #AWSStudyGroup #FCAJ #FirstCloudJourney #AWSLambda #AmazonS3 #OCR #ONNX #Serverless #TiengViet

title: Deploying the Backend Stack with AWS SAM
content:
The askfirst-dev stack is described in infra/template.yaml. In this section we create the “ingestion and orchestration” part of the system. The ai Lambda is handled separately in 5.5.
Created Name on AWS Notes Lambda webhook (Java 21, Function URL) askfirst-dev-webhook Receives Telegram updates, checks the secret header Lambda worker (Java 21, alias live) askfirst-dev-worker Reads jobs from SQS, invokes ai, sends results Lambda worker-dlq (Java 21) askfirst-dev-worker-dlq Handles jobs that landed in the DLQ, notifies the user DynamoDB table (PK/SK, GSI1, TTL, PITR, on-demand) askfirst-dev One table for every record type SQS queue + DLQ askfirst-dev-jobs, askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq Visibility timeout of 720 seconds, moved to the DLQ after 5 attempts S3 data bucket askfirst-dev-data-<ACCOUNT_ID> Public access blocked, encrypted, donated/ auto-deleted after 30 days CloudWatch alarm askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty Fires when the DLQ has a job SSM configuration parameters /askfirst/dev/... Table name, queue URL, bucket name Step 1: Create the secrets in SSM before deploying The template does not create secrets; you create them manually so their values never appear in the template. Enter the token via Read-Host so it does not end up in the PowerShell history:
$env:AWS_PROFILE = "ai2test"; $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $t = Read-Host "Telegram bot token" aws ssm put-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token --type SecureString --value $t --overwrite Remove-Variable t # webhook secret: random string containing only A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - $s = -join ((48..57 + 65..90 + 97..122) | Get-Random -Count 48 | ForEach-Object { [char]$_ }) aws ssm put-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/webhook_secret --type SecureString --value $s --overwrite Remove-Variable s The template also reads the hash of the privacy policy at deploy time ({{resolve:ssm:...}}), so this parameter must exist beforehand as well:
$sha = (Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 docs/privacy-policy.md).Hash.ToLower() aws ssm put-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/config/policy_sha256 --type String --value $sha --overwrite This hash is the “version” of the terms the user consents to in the bot. Changing the policy file changes the hash, and the bot will ask users to consent again.
Step 2: Create an SNS topic for the alarm An alarm with no recipient is useless: in my first test, the DLQ alarm transitioned to ALARM but nobody knew because AlarmActions was empty. Create the topic and subscribe an email first:
$topic = aws sns create-topic --name askfirst-dev-alarms --query TopicArn --output text aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $topic --protocol email --notification-endpoint <YOUR_EMAIL> Open the email and click Confirm subscription, otherwise SNS will not send anything.
Step 3: Build the 3 Java Lambda functions SAM builds each Java function independently, so the common module must first be installed into the local Maven repository (~/.m2):
cd backend\ScamProtection .\mvnw.cmd clean install -DskipTests # about 30 seconds, must end with BUILD SUCCESS cd ..\.. If Maven is not installed, create an mvn shim for SAM (once):
New-Item -ItemType Directory "$env:TEMP\mvnshim" -Force | Out-Null Set-Content "$env:TEMP\mvnshim\mvn.cmd" "@echo off`r`ncall `"$PWD\backend\ScamProtection\mvnw.cmd`" %*" $env:PATH = "$env:TEMP\mvnshim;$env:PATH" Step 4: Build and deploy the stack cd infra sam build # 1–2 minutes, must end with Build Succeeded $tok = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text sam deploy --parameter-overrides Stage=dev ` TelegramBotUsername=askfirst_ai2_test_bot ` "TelegramBotToken=$tok" ` "AlarmTopicArn=$topic" Remove-Variable tok The stack name, Region, and CAPABILITY_IAM are already set in infra/samconfig.toml. TelegramBotToken is a NoEcho parameter: CloudFormation shows **** instead of the value. It must be passed again on every redeploy, otherwise worker loses the token (the default value is an empty string). --parameter-overrides on the command line completely replaces the parameter_overrides line in samconfig.toml, so always pass the full set of parameters. No changes to deploy means there is nothing new in the code; it is not an error. Step 5: Quick verification with the CLI # Stack outputs aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name askfirst-dev ` --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[].[OutputKey,OutputValue]" --output table # DynamoDB: both TTL and PITR enabled aws dynamodb describe-time-to-live --table-name askfirst-dev aws dynamodb describe-continuous-backups --table-name askfirst-dev ` --query "ContinuousBackupsDescription.PointInTimeRecoveryDescription.PointInTimeRecoveryStatus" # SQS: 720 seconds and moved to the DLQ after 5 attempts $q = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/sqs/jobs_queue_url --query Parameter.Value --output text aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $q --attribute-names VisibilityTimeout RedrivePolicy # Alarm wired to SNS aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty ` --query "MetricAlarms[0].[StateValue,AlarmActions]" The stack has 14 output keys; those used in later sections are WebhookFunctionUrl (5.6), WorkerRoleArn and JobsDlqUrl (5.7).
When the deployment fails Symptom Resolution sam build reports that mvn cannot be found The shim from step 3 is not on PATH, or you are running in Git Bash. Rerun in PowerShell. Error resolving policy_sha256 The parameter from step 1 was not created, or was created in the wrong Region. Stack in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE after the first deployment CloudFormation locks the stack in this state. Delete the stack (empty the askfirst-dev-data-... bucket first, then run sam delete --stack-name askfirst-dev), fix the error, and deploy from scratch. Viewing why a resource failed aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name askfirst-dev --query "StackEvents[?ResourceStatus=='CREATE_FAILED'].[LogicalResourceId,ResourceStatusReason]" --output table

title: Packaging and Deploying the AI Lambda
content:
The ai Lambda is the heaviest part: Python 3.12, ONNX Runtime, RapidOCR, sentencepiece, boto3. In this section we build the image ourselves with Docker locally, push it to ECR, and then create the function with the AWS CLI using a least-privilege role. This is exactly how the team’s shared environment runs: worker invokes askfirst-dev-ai:live by name, so this function does not need to be part of the SAM stack.
infra/template.yaml also contains an ai function (only created when the AiImageUri parameter is passed). If you want everything in a single stack, after step 2 you can run sam deploy with AiImageUri=<image URI> in place of steps 3–5. I chose to create it with the CLI to keep control over versions and aliases while testing each revision of the AI part.
Step 1: Create the ECR repository $env:AWS_PROFILE = "ai2test"; $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $acct = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text $reg = "$acct.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" aws ecr create-repository --repository-name askfirst-dev-ai --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true aws ecr get-login-password | docker login -u AWS --password-stdin $reg The ECR login token expires after 12 hours; if a push fails with no basic auth credentials, rerun the last line.
Step 2: Build the image and push it to ECR Start Docker Desktop first. Build from the repo root, because the image needs kb/ and prompts/, not just ai/:
$sha = git rev-parse --short HEAD $img = "${reg}/askfirst-dev-ai:main-$sha" docker build --platform linux/amd64 --provenance=false -f ai/Dockerfile -t $img . docker push $img Three points in ai/Dockerfile that I had to fix when building the first version:
Point Reason Keep the repo’s directory tree under /var/task (ai/src, ai/config, kb, prompts) The code locates prompts/ and config/models.yaml via paths relative to the .py file. Installing the package into site-packages makes these two folders “disappear” at runtime. --platform linux/amd64 The embedder is an int8 build optimized for x86; arm64 has not been measured. --provenance=false Recent Docker versions push attestations as a manifest list, which Lambda does not accept. The first build takes about 15 minutes (the image is about 1.4 GB); subsequent builds take 1–4 minutes thanks to the cache, since usually only the ai/src layer changes.
Step 3: Create a least-privilege IAM role The ai role only needs to: write logs, read the model bucket, read/write a few cache keys in the table, read exactly one SSM parameter (the bot token, to download images from Telegram itself), and call Bedrock.
$trust = '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"lambda.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' aws iam create-role --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role --assume-role-policy-document $trust aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role ` --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole aws iam put-role-policy --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role --policy-name ai-least-privilege ` --policy-document file://ai-policy.json Contents of ai-policy.json (replace <ACCOUNT_ID>):
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Artifacts", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::askfirst-ai2-test-<ACCOUNT_ID>/*" }, { "Sid": "Cache", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem"], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:table/askfirst-dev" }, { "Sid": "BotToken", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ssm:GetParameter", "Resource": "arn:aws:ssm:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:parameter/askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token" }, { "Sid": "Bedrock", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:ApplyGuardrail"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-2::foundation-model/qwen.qwen3-32b-v1:0", "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-2::foundation-model/openai.gpt-oss-120b-1:0", "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-2:<ACCOUNT_ID>:guardrail/*"] } ] } The role has no s3:PutObject, no dynamodb:Scan/DeleteItem, and cannot read any other SSM parameter. The token is encrypted with the AWS managed key alias/aws/ssm; this key allows decryption through SSM, so no additional kms:Decrypt is needed.
In the team’s environment, Bedrock is in a different account, so the Bedrock statement is replaced with sts:AssumeRole on that account’s askfirst-bedrock-from-team role, and the function has an extra BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN variable. When working in a single account, use the policy above as is.
Step 4: Create the function aws lambda create-function --function-name askfirst-dev-ai ` --package-type Image --code ImageUri=$img ` --role "arn:aws:iam::${acct}:role/askfirst-ai2test-ai-role" ` --architectures x86_64 --memory-size 3008 --timeout 90 --ephemeral-storage Size=1024 ` --environment "Variables={PIPELINE_IMPL=real,ARTIFACT_BUCKET=askfirst-ai2-test-$acct,TABLE_NAME=askfirst-dev,BOT_TOKEN_PARAM=/askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token}" aws lambda wait function-active-v2 --function-name askfirst-dev-ai Why these numbers:
Setting Value Reason Memory 3008 MB Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to memory (about 1,769 MB = 1 vCPU). I measured 3 settings: 1769 MB made the INIT phase hit the 10-second limit, 2048 MB had a 7.1-second INIT, 3008 MB had a 6.2-second INIT. Actual RAM usage is only about 0.8–1 GB; what is needed is CPU. Timeout 90 seconds worker has a 120-second timeout and still has to send the Telegram message after ai responds. Ephemeral storage 1024 MB The models downloaded to /tmp/artifacts total about 250 MB. PIPELINE_IMPL=real Runs the real pipeline; stub only replies based on keywords, used to keep the bot working when the pipeline is broken. Step 5: Publish a version and create the live alias worker always invokes askfirst-dev-ai:live. The alias lets you switch the running version (or roll back) without touching worker:
$v = aws lambda publish-version --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --description "main $sha" --query Version --output text aws lambda create-alias --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --name live --function-version $v Updating to a new version (whenever main has changes in the AI part):
aws lambda update-function-code --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --image-uri $img aws lambda wait function-updated-v2 --function-name askfirst-dev-ai $v = aws lambda publish-version --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --description "main $sha" --query Version --output text aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --qualifier $v --query State # wait for "Active" aws lambda update-alias --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --name live --function-version $v Rolling back: aws lambda update-alias --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --name live --function-version <OLD_VERSION>. This only works while the old version’s image is still in ECR, so do not delete the image of any version you might need to roll back to.
Step 6: Test-invoke with a sample request contracts/fixtures/ contains the sample requests that CI also uses. Take the request part of the OTP case and invoke the live alias:
(Get-Content contracts/fixtures/analyze/otp.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json).request | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content -Encoding utf8 payload.json aws lambda invoke --function-name askfirst-dev-ai:live ` --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload fileb://payload.json out.json Get-Content out.json You should see "StatusCode": 200, and out.json should contain "op": "analyze" with risk level DANGEROUS for the message “Gửi mã OTP cho tôi” (“Send me the OTP code”). The first invocation is a cold start, so it is much slower than subsequent ones (measurements in 5.7).
Check the startup logs to make sure all three models were preloaded during the INIT phase:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-ai --since 15m --format short | Select-String "rag_warm|ocr_warm|vietocr_warm|Init Duration" You must see rag_warm, ocr_warm, and vietocr_warm, all with status ok.

title: Workshop
content:
Building a Production Environment for Ask First on a Single AWS Account: From AI Models on S3 to a Telegram Bot Ask First (“Hỏi Trước”) is a Telegram bot that helps older adults check a suspicious message, link, or screenshot before acting on it. The bot replies in Vietnamese: how risky the message is, which scam pattern it resembles, and what to do right away.
This workshop follows the exact path I took when building the team’s shared runtime environment on my personal AWS account (from 19/11/2026): deploy each component to AWS, test it, and only then wire everything into the full pipeline. That order means that when something fails, we immediately know which component is at fault.
By the end of the workshop, you will have:
an S3 bucket holding the AI models (OCR, VietOCR, embedder) and the knowledge base index, with SHA-256 verification; an AWS SAM stack with 3 Java Lambda functions (webhook, worker, worker-dlq), DynamoDB, SQS with a DLQ, and a CloudWatch alarm that sends email through SNS; an ai Lambda function (Python 3.12, container image on Amazon ECR) that runs OCR, masks personal data, applies the rule set, performs RAG, and calls Amazon Bedrock; a Telegram bot that gives real answers, along with logs, alarms, and measurements that prove the system works correctly. All commands in this workshop are run in PowerShell on Windows, since that is the machine I deploy from. AWS CLI commands are identical on macOS/Linux; only the variable syntax differs ($env:X = "..." instead of export X=...).
Contents Overview and architecture Preparing the account and tools Uploading AI models to S3 Deploying the backend stack with AWS SAM Packaging and deploying the AI Lambda Connecting the Telegram bot Testing and measurement Monitoring and alerting Cost and optimization Cleaning up resources Demo and lessons learned

title: Connecting the Telegram Bot
content:
At this point every component is on AWS. What remains is to tell Telegram to send updates to the webhook Function URL, along with a secret known only to us and Telegram.
Step 1: Verify the webhook’s protection before opening it to Telegram The Function URL is public (AuthType: NONE): anyone who knows the URL can send requests. The protection lives in the code: any request without an X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header matching the secret in SSM is rejected. Test all three cases:
$url = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name askfirst-dev ` --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='WebhookFunctionUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $sec = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/webhook_secret --with-decryption ` --query Parameter.Value --output text curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "no secret: %{http_code}`n" -X POST $url -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{}" curl.exe -s -o NUL -w "wrong secret: %{http_code}`n" -X POST $url -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: wrong" -d "{}" curl.exe -s -w " | right secret: %{http_code}`n" -X POST $url -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: $sec" -d "{}" Remove-Variable sec Results on my environment (27/11/2026):
no secret: 401 wrong secret: 401 IGNORED | right secret: 200 IGNORED is correct: the secret is valid but the body is empty and not a Telegram update, so webhook ignores it.
Step 2: Register the webhook with Telegram The scripts/set_webhook.py script calls setWebhook with the URL, the secret, and the list of update types to receive. Pass values through environment variables of the current window, not through a .env file:
$env:TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text $env:TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/webhook_secret --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text python scripts/set_webhook.py --url $url python scripts/set_commands.py # command menu: /batdau, /huongdan, /caidat, /nguoithan, /lichsu, /bilua Remove-Item Env:TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, Env:TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET The script refuses to run without a secret: a webhook without a secret lets anyone forge Telegram updates.
Verify on the Telegram side with getWebhookInfo (URL redacted):
{ "url": "https://<FUNCTION_URL>", "has_custom_certificate": false, "pending_update_count": 0, "max_connections": 40, "allowed_updates": ["message", "callback_query", "my_chat_member"] } A pending_update_count of 0 means Telegram has no updates waiting to be redelivered; this number grows when webhook returns errors. my_chat_member tells the bot when a user blocks it.
The Function URL only changes when the stack is deleted and recreated. Redeploying code does not require re-registering the webhook.
Step 3: Send the first message Open the bot and send /start. The bot sends a greeting with the terms and a consent button. Under Vietnam’s Personal Data Protection Law and Decree 356/2025/ND-CP (effective from 01/01/2026), consent must be verifiable, so the bot only processes messages after the user actively taps the consent button. Tap consent. Forward or type a suspected scam message. The bot replies “⏳” almost instantly, then edits that same message into the result. If the bot does not reply Symptom Where to look Not even a “⏳” getWebhookInfo: last_error_message and pending_update_count. Logs in /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-webhook. “⏳” appears but no result Logs in /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-worker: look for job_failed or invalid_job lines. Depth of the askfirst-dev-jobs queue. Text messages work, images fail ai downloads images using the token read from BOT_TOKEN_PARAM. An old token or a wrong parameter breaks only images; text messages still work. A result arrives but says “chỉ kiểm được dấu hiệu cơ bản” (“only basic signs could be checked”) The LLM is turned off (kill switch llm_enabled=false) or Bedrock is failing; the pipeline falls back to rules-only mode.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall impressions What I remember most about FCAJ is building a product that actually runs on AWS instead of isolated exercises. Ask First forced me to solve problems that are not in any syllabus: an OCR model dropping Vietnamese letters, a Lambda that must load models before any user arrives, and a shared environment that needs someone to keep permissions and secrets in order. That is where I learned the most.
I also got used to working like a development team: every change goes through a PR, with review, measurements and an eval gate on CI.
Satisfaction level Satisfied: 4/5.
Satisfied with the hands-on environment: real AWS usage, an office to work from, and events to attend. Events such as the Buildrathon Kickoff and Student Community Day let me meet practitioners and students from other universities. Not a full 5/5 because of guidance in the first weeks; it took me time to know what to focus on for the AI role. What could be improved A suggested learning path per role (AI, backend) for the first 2–3 weeks. A mid-term architecture review with a mentor, so teams catch weak design choices early. Clearer guidance on cost and permission management when teams set up their own AWS account. Would I recommend it to friends? Yes. I would recommend FCAJ to software engineering students who want to work in cloud or AI, because:
The program has you build a real product with a clear target user, not just theory. You work with AWS services in a real operating context: Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, Bedrock. Teamwork follows a PR, review and CI process similar to industry. I would tell friends to prepare basic AWS and Git knowledge beforehand, so they do not lose the first weeks the way I did.

title: Testing and Measurement
content:
I test in three layers, from the inside out: invoke the ai Lambda directly with sample requests, send real messages through the bot, and then deliberately break a component to see how the system reacts.
5.7.1 Invoking the ai Lambda directly with sample requests The script below invokes the live alias with each request in contracts/fixtures/ and reads the REPORT line from the returned log (LogType=Tail) to get the duration and memory usage:
import base64, json, re, boto3, pathlib lam = boto3.Session(profile_name="ai2test", region_name="ap-southeast-1").client("lambda") fx = pathlib.Path("contracts/fixtures/analyze") for name in ["otp", "default", "link", "smalltalk", "unreadable"]: req = json.loads((fx / f"{name}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["request"] r = lam.invoke(FunctionName="askfirst-dev-ai:live", Payload=json.dumps(req).encode(), LogType="Tail") body = json.loads(r["Payload"].read()) report = re.search(r"Duration: ([\d.]+) ms.*Max Memory Used: (\d+) MB", base64.b64decode(r["LogResult"]).decode(), re.S) v = body["analyze"]["verdict"] print(name, v["level"], v["path"], report.groups()) Results from 27/11/2026 on the latest version (commit e3027ff, LLM enabled):
Request Risk level Processing path Lambda duration Notes otp (“Gửi mã OTP cho tôi” — “Send me the OTP code”), cold start DANGEROUS llm INIT 8.7 s + 2.4 s First invocation after a period of inactivity default (greeting message) LOW_RISK escalated 4.1 s Rules not confident enough; the judge also consulted the fallback model link (message with a link) SUSPICIOUS escalated 10.5 s Includes probing the shortened link smalltalk LOW_RISK fast 11 ms No LLM call unreadable UNSURE fast 10 ms No LLM call default, second invocation LOW_RISK cache 6 ms Verdict retrieved from DynamoDB Request missing the op field error unknown_op 2 ms Returns a structured error, no crash render (building the reply message) 88 ms Template assembly only Maximum memory used was 930 MB out of 3008 MB. Invocations that use the LLM also return a cost estimate for that invocation (cost_usd_est, about 0.0014 USD for the default case), along with the duration of each step (latency_ms: rules, RAG, guard, judge).
5.7.2 Choosing memory by measurement, not guesswork I deployed the same image at three memory settings and triggered one cold start at each (19/11/2026, with RAG + OCR preloading in the INIT phase already enabled):
Memory vCPU (estimated) INIT Image when warm Conclusion 1769 MB 1 hit the 10 s limit Lambda cut INIT short and reran it in the invocation: the first message took 35 s 2048 MB ~1.2 7.1 s 2.9–4.2 s Works, but close to the limit 3008 MB ~1.7 6.2 s 2.5–2.7 s Chosen Actual RAM usage was only about 0.8 GB at all three settings, so increasing memory here is about buying CPU, not RAM. Each setting was measured only once, so INIT figures may vary: today, after adding VietOCR, INIT at 3008 MB is 8.7 s.
5.7.3 End-to-end testing through the real bot Scenario How Expected result Result Scam text message Send a message impersonating the police demanding a transfer to a “safe account” “⏳” then edited into DANGEROUS Pass (screenshot in 5.6) Message batching Send 2 messages 0.5 s apart One “⏳”, one combined result for both messages Pass (24/11): the first job was dropped (skip=stale), the second job analyzed both messages Screenshot Send a screenshot of a fake bank SMS with the link i-vietcombank.com OCR reads the link correctly, URL intel catches the fake domain Pass (24/11): DANGEROUS, 11.7 s when warm Shortened link Message with tinyurl.com/... pointing to a fake bank domain The bot probes it with HEAD and sees the real domain behind it Pass (23/11): DANGEROUS 80, 0.39 s Shortened link pointing to an internal IP Link pointing to 169.254.169.254.nip.io No connection to the target (SSRF protection) Pass: domain recorded only, not opened I use two log sources for cross-checking: the worker and ai logs share the same trace_id, so filtering by one trace_id shows the entire journey of a single check.
5.7.4 Failure scenario: blocking the ai Lambda Goal: prove that when the analysis part is completely down, the user is still notified and the operations team receives an email.
# 1. Block ai: with reserved concurrency = 0, every invocation is rejected aws lambda put-function-concurrency --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --reserved-concurrent-executions 0 # 2. Shorten the wait between retries to speed up the test (default 720 s) $q = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/sqs/jobs_queue_url --query Parameter.Value --output text aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $q --attributes VisibilityTimeout=150 # 3. Send a message to the bot, then wait about 15–20 minutes # 4. RESTORE the configuration after the test aws lambda delete-function-concurrency --function-name askfirst-dev-ai aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $q --attributes VisibilityTimeout=720 Results (24/11/2026):
worker retried 5 times, each failing with AiException:invoke. On the 5th attempt, worker edited the “⏳” message into “Dạ, hiện cháu đang bận…” (“Sorry, I’m busy right now…”). The job went to the DLQ. worker-dlq saw that this job had already been reported, logged already_handled, and did not send a second busy message. A message B sent in the meantime kept its own “⏳”; once ai was unblocked, B produced a normal result. The askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty alarm transitioned to ALARM. Steps 3 and 4 cover two bugs I found during the first test (20/11): worker-dlq sent a second “busy” message and could mistakenly edit the “⏳” of a different message. I reported them to the backend team with reproduction steps; the team’s fix passes this exact scenario.
5.7.5 Testing outside AWS Before each deployment, the AI part must pass the test suite locally and in CI:
cd ai uv run ruff check . uv run pytest -q # 835 tests at commit 41014e0 (PR #178) The repo’s CI additionally runs OCR bench (measures OCR on 66 labeled images) and Eval gate (compares rule-set results against the base branch on a labeled sample set) for every pull request.

title: Monitoring and Alerting
content:
The system has no server to log in to, so all operational information comes from three CloudWatch sources: logs (what happened in each invocation), metrics (trends), and alarms (when human intervention is needed).
5.8.1 Logs: one JSON line per invocation Each function writes to the log group /aws/lambda/<function name>. The ai Lambda writes exactly one JSON line per invocation, containing only metadata:
{"trace_id": "01J00000000000000000000000", "op": "analyze", "cache_hit": false, "result": "ok", "ms": 10532} {"trace_id": "01J00000000000000000000000", "op": null, "result": "fatal/unknown_op", "cause": null, "ms": 0} On the Java side, worker writes a corresponding line with the same trace_id:
ai_invoke op=analyze trace=01M8DHECPQPYAKEC6M37EXPB82 ms=502 outcome=ok ai_invoke op=render trace=01M8DHECPQPYAKEC6M37EXPB82 ms=162 outcome=ok Logs do not contain message content, phone numbers, tokens, or Telegram file download URLs. I verified this by scanning the logs for the exact content of the test messages and for the token string: no matches.
Set a log retention period. By default, log groups keep logs forever, and CloudWatch charges for storage per GB-month. Set 14 days for all 4 log groups:
foreach ($f in "webhook","worker","worker-dlq","ai") { aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name "/aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-$f" --retention-in-days 14 } 5.8.2 Querying with CloudWatch Logs Insights The three queries I use most, run against the /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-ai log group.
Overall health (cold starts, duration, memory):
filter @type = "REPORT" | stats count(*) as invocations, count(@initDuration) as coldStarts, avg(@duration) as avgMs, pct(@duration, 95) as p95Ms, max(@initDuration) as maxInitMs, max(@maxMemoryUsed/1000/1000) as maxMemMB Results for the 7 days up to 27/11/2026 (after running the test cases in 5.7):
invocations coldStarts avgMs p95Ms maxInitMs maxMemMB 252 21 2,095 7,499 9,552 1,612 A maxInitMs of 9.55 seconds is the number to watch most closely: the INIT phase has a hard 10-second limit (see the lessons in 5.11).
Are the models preloaded during the INIT phase:
filter @message like /_warm/ | parse @message /"event": "(?<ev>[a-z_]+)"/ | stats count(*) by ev Result: rag_warm 23, ocr_warm 22, vietocr_warm 19 times. The counts differ because older versions did not yet preload OCR or VietOCR.
Following a single check across multiple functions: select both the worker and ai log groups, then
fields @timestamp, @log, @message | filter @message like /01M8DHECPQPYAKEC6M37EXPB82/ | sort @timestamp asc 5.8.3 Metrics to watch Metric Namespace Meaning for Ask First Errors, Throttles of askfirst-dev-ai AWS/Lambda The AI pipeline is failing or being throttled by concurrency limits Duration (p95) of askfirst-dev-ai AWS/Lambda Image messages slowing down (OCR) or Bedrock being slow ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage of askfirst-dev-jobs AWS/SQS Jobs are stuck: users are staring at “⏳” NumberOfMessagesSent of askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq AWS/SQS A job has failed permanently after 5 attempts 5.8.4 DLQ alarm sending email The stack creates the askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty alarm, which transitions to ALARM when a job lands in the DLQ. Because worker-dlq takes messages out of the DLQ almost immediately, the DLQ depth always appears to be 0; the alarm is the only way to know a job has failed.
An alarm is only useful if someone receives it. In 5.4 we passed AlarmTopicArn at deploy time; verify it:
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty ` --query "MetricAlarms[0].[StateValue,AlarmActions[0]]" --output text aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn <TOPIC_ARN> --query "Subscriptions[].[Protocol,SubscriptionArn]" --output text SubscriptionArn must be a full ARN; if it is PendingConfirmation, the email has not been confirmed yet.
To test the alarm without waiting for a real failure:
aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty ` --state-value ALARM --state-reason "Test alarm email" The email arrives within about a minute; the alarm returns to OK on its own at the next evaluation period.
