title: Cost and Optimization
content:
This section answers two questions: how much building and testing the system actually cost, and how much running 3,000 checks per month (the project’s target load) would cost. What sets this estimate apart: Lambda durations come from measurements on real Lambda (5.7, 5.8), not from a dev machine.
5.9.1 Actual cost of building and testing Cost Explorer, filtered by RECORD_TYPE = Usage (usage cost before credits), 01–26/11/2026, whole account:
Service USD AWS Cost Explorer (API) 0.0700 Amazon ECR 0.0168 Amazon Bedrock 0.0061 Amazon S3 0.0022 Amazon DynamoDB 0.0005 AWS Lambda 0.0003 SQS, SNS, CloudWatch, KMS, CloudFormation 0 (within the Free Tier) Total ≈ 0.096, fully covered by credits, amount due 0 USD Two takeaways:
The largest item turned out to be the Cost Explorer API: each ce:GetCostAndUsage call costs 0.01 USD, and I called it many times while writing the report. Viewing costs in the console is free; only call the API when you need automation. ECR is the only time-based charge: each ai image takes about 0.36 GB at 0.10 USD/GB-month. Keeping many old tags costs money steadily even though nobody uses them. Bedrock is small in the table above because most of the team’s LLM calls run in the separate Bedrock account (5.1).
5.9.2 Assumptions for 3,000 checks per month Assumption Value Source Text / image ratio 70% / 30% Assumption Checks that call the LLM 75% (25% go through the fast path or cache) Assumption based on the design; actual ratio not yet measured ai analyzing text with LLM 4.1 s Measured on Lambda 27/11 (5.7.1) ai analyzing an image with LLM 9 s 5.5 s OCR + rules measured on Lambda 24/11, plus about 3.5 s for the judge ai building the reply (render) 0.09 s Measured on Lambda 27/11 worker equal to ai duration + 0.6 s for sending to Telegram worker waits for ai to return SQS requests 0.91 million/month Measured: 211,401 empty receives in 7 days (Lambda long polling), extrapolated to 30 days LLM tokens per check 0.000792 USD Measured by the team with the judge_v3 prompt (docs/results/cost-estimate.md) From this: ai runs about 14,050 seconds/month in total across 6,000 invocations, i.e. an average of 2,342 ms per invocation; worker has 6,000 invocations averaging 2,642 ms.
5.9.3 Estimate with the AWS Pricing Calculator Public estimate: https://calculator.aws/#/estimate?id=307350af77a0dacdf746bb155387741aead2ec84 (created 27/11/2026, Singapore Region, “Without Free Tier” selected for each item to avoid double-counting the Free Tier).
The Calculator does not yet offer Qwen3 (or gpt-oss) in Sydney, so Bedrock is calculated by hand using unit prices from the AWS Price List API.
Component Input / calculation USD/month, no Free Tier With always-free Lambda ai (3008 MB, x86) 6,000 requests × 2,342 ms, /tmp 1024 MB 0.69 0 Lambda worker (512 MB) 6,000 requests × 2,642 ms 0.13 0 Lambda webhook (512 MB) 6,000 requests × 300 ms 0.01 0 SQS (jobs + DLQ) 0.91 million requests 0.36 0 DynamoDB on-demand 1 GB, 15,000 writes + 15,000 reads 0.29 ≈ 0.01 S3 1 GB, 500 PUT, 2,000 GET 0.03 0.03 ECR 1.1 GB (keeping 3 images) 0.11 0.11 CloudWatch 0.05 GB logs, 1 alarm 0.14 0 Bedrock LLM (calculated by hand) 2,250 checks × 0.000792 USD 1.78 1.78 Bedrock Guardrails (calculated by hand) 2,250 checks × 0.15 USD / 1,000 text units 0.34 0.34 SNS email, SSM Parameter Store standard ≈ 0 0 Total ≈ 3.88 ≈ 2.27 The “With always-free” column subtracts the non-expiring free tiers: Lambda 1 million requests + 400,000 GB-seconds, SQS 1 million requests, CloudWatch 10 alarms + 5 GB of logs, DynamoDB 25 GB of storage. These tiers are shared across the whole account.
Observations: more than half of the cost is the LLM. The AWS infrastructure part (Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, S3, ECR, CloudWatch) is only about 1.8 USD/month without the Free Tier, and close to 0 with it. Each check costs about 0.0013 USD (3.88 USD / 3,000 checks), or about 33 VND.
5.9.4 Optimization measures Measure Savings Status No VPC/NAT Gateway: every Lambda calls AWS services through encrypted public endpoints About 32 USD/month for the NAT Gateway alone Applied Fully serverless, DynamoDB on-demand: no hourly-billed components Cost drops to 0 when there are no messages Applied Fast path + 24-hour cache: skip the LLM when the rules are confident or the content has already been checked ≈ 0.00094 USD per skipped check (tokens + Guardrail) Applied Kill switch llm_enabled=false in DynamoDB: turn off the LLM under spam or when hitting the budget Caps Bedrock spending Applied Choosing memory by measurement (3008 MB) instead of over-provisioning No paying for unused RAM Applied (5.7.2) 14-day log retention Stops log storage costs from growing month after month Command in 5.8.1 ECR lifecycle policy keeping the 3 latest images Each old image ≈ 0.036 USD/month Command below AWS Budgets at 50 USD/month, alerts at 80% and 100% Early detection of unusual spending Applied (5.2) ECR lifecycle policy keeping the 3 most recent images:
$rule = '{"rules":[{"rulePriority":1,"description":"keep last 3","selection":{"tagStatus":"any","countType":"imageCountMoreThan","countNumber":3},"action":{"type":"expire"}}]}' aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name askfirst-dev-ai --lifecycle-policy-text $rule Before enabling it, check which image the live alias (and any version you may need to roll back to) is using: once an image is deleted, you can no longer roll back to that version.

content: Week 9 objectives Build a RAG that runs locally inside Lambda with no external embedding service (AI-29), then wire it into RealPipeline (INT-03). Put eval into CI so that any PR that breaks the rules or the KB is caught (AI-09). Contribute human scores to AI1’s LLM-as-a-judge experiment (AI-11). Tasks this week Day Task Start date Completion date Reference Mon - Build a corpus of scam warnings from .gov.vn sites and newspapers for RAG 09/11/2026 11/11/2026 kb/alerts.yaml Tue - Write the e5-small int8 embedder, build_index.py and the retriever; measure Recall@4 10/11/2026 11/11/2026 PR #147 Wed - Open and merge local RAG (#147) - Hand-score 20 AI-11 samples with the rubric, before looking at the LLM scores (#146) - Open the PR wiring RAG into RealPipeline + artifact upload script (#151) and the CI eval gate PR (#153) - Review AI1’s batch of PRs: Bedrock Qwen3 32B spike (#132), 4-model benchmark (#133), outputConfig (#134), Guardrails (#135), LLM-as-a-judge (#136), red-team (#137), Gemini reference (#141), fallback model (#142), judge fixes (#144, #145 approved), OTP/ID-card rules (#149), G1 hand scoring (#150) 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 PR #146, PR #147, #151, #153 Thu - Fix after review and merge #151, #153; the eval gate ran for real on a PR and commented a comparison table 12/11/2026 12/11/2026 PR #151, PR #153 Fri - Start the bot message wording (SH-08) using a reading sheet for older users 13/11/2026 13/11/2026 PR #157 Sat - Review 2 BE2 PRs: the “Bot was wrong” flow (BE-30, #155) and /rutdongy data deletion (BE-31, #156) 14/11/2026 14/11/2026 #155, #156 Results Local RAG (#147): a corpus of 103 warnings; scenario-card Recall@4 on real_scam 35/38 = 92.1% (threshold 90%); query p50 7.9 ms, p95 9.7 ms on a laptop, about 57 ms for a 512-token message. RAG wired into the pipeline (#151): cites up to 3 warnings matching the verdict’s scenario code; if model loading fails, it continues without RAG and logs no message content. CI eval gate (#153): runs eval on the base branch and the PR and compares with the baseline; without a Bedrock role it runs rules only and blocks when the result is more than 2 points worse than the baseline. Reviewed 15 PRs this week (13 from AI1, 2 from BE2). Lessons learned With rules only, recall is only about 19%, so the absolute 90% threshold cannot apply; comparing with the baseline is what catches PRs that break the rules (#153). The retriever’s top-3 score aggregation was chosen on the same benchmark, so Recall@4 needs an independent set to be more trustworthy.

title: Cleaning Up Resources
content:
The system costs almost nothing when there are no messages, but a few storage-based charges remain (ECR, S3, logs), as do secrets that are still valid. After finishing the workshop, clean up in exactly the order below. The order matters because: CloudFormation cannot delete a bucket that still contains objects; the ai Lambda and resources created with the CLI are not part of the stack, so sam delete does not touch them.
Steps 3–7 are irreversible: the DynamoDB table (including PITR backups), the models on S3, the images, and the bot token are all lost. The team’s environment is the shared runtime environment until the end of the program, so I have not yet run this section on it; the commands below are the procedure I will use at the end.
$env:AWS_PROFILE = "ai2test"; $env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $acct = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text Step 1: Disconnect Telegram from the system Remove the webhook first so Telegram stops sending updates to the Function URL while deletion is in progress:
$env:TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN = aws ssm get-parameter --name /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text python scripts/set_webhook.py --delete Remove-Item Env:TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN Step 2: Delete the ai Lambda and its role (created with the CLI in 5.5) aws lambda delete-alias --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --name live aws lambda delete-function --function-name askfirst-dev-ai # also deletes all versions aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role --policy-name ai-least-privilege aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role ` --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole aws iam delete-role --role-name askfirst-ai2test-ai-role Step 3: Delete the ECR images and repository aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name askfirst-dev-ai --force # --force also deletes the images inside Step 4: Empty and delete the buckets aws s3 rm "s3://askfirst-ai2-test-$acct" --recursive aws s3 rb "s3://askfirst-ai2-test-$acct" aws s3 rm "s3://askfirst-dev-data-$acct" --recursive # this bucket was created by the stack, just empty it Step 5: Delete the SAM stack sam delete --stack-name askfirst-dev --no-prompts aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name askfirst-dev # must report "does not exist" This command deletes the 3 Java Lambda functions, the DynamoDB table, the 2 queues, the alarm, the (now empty) data bucket, and the SSM configuration parameters created by the stack. If sam delete fails on DataBucket, go back to step 4.
Step 6: Delete manually created items outside the stack # Secrets and the policy hash (created in 5.4 step 1) aws ssm delete-parameters --names /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token /askfirst/dev/telegram/webhook_secret /askfirst/dev/config/policy_sha256 # The alarm's SNS topic (5.4 step 2) aws sns delete-topic --topic-arn "arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:${acct}:askfirst-dev-alarms" # Log groups are not deleted along with the functions foreach ($f in "webhook","worker","worker-dlq","ai") { aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name "/aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-$f" } # The bucket SAM uses for deployment packages (if no other stack uses SAM) aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name aws-sam-cli-managed-default --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[0].OutputValue" --output text The aws-sam-cli-managed-default-samclisourcebucket-... bucket has versioning enabled, so you must also delete the old versions in the console (Empty) before deleting the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack.
Step 7: Revoke access In @BotFather: /revoke the bot token (or /deletebot if it is no longer needed). IAM → Users → ai2-dev → Security credentials: deactivate and then delete the access key used for the workshop. Keep AWS Budgets for one more month to make sure no charges remain, then delete it if you wish. Final check aws lambda list-functions --query "Functions[?starts_with(FunctionName,'askfirst-dev')].FunctionName" aws dynamodb list-tables --query "TableNames[?starts_with(@,'askfirst')]" aws sqs list-queues --queue-name-prefix askfirst-dev aws ecr describe-repositories --query "repositories[?starts_with(repositoryName,'askfirst')].repositoryName" aws s3 ls | Select-String askfirst aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /askfirst --recursive --query "Parameters[].Name" Every command must return an empty list. A few days later, open Billing → Bills to make sure there are no new charges for Lambda, ECR, or S3.

Lessons learned Only measuring on a real Lambda revealed the 17–19 s cold start; the dev machine does not have this problem. Preloading models at INIT makes every cold start longer, in exchange for a first message that does not wait long (#173). The Lambda INIT phase has a 10 s ceiling; at 1769 MB (about 1 vCPU) the models cannot load in time. Memory is the only way to get more CPU. Testing the DLQ by deliberately blocking the Lambda uncovered a bug that sent the “busy” message twice, which unit tests did not catch (#42).

title: Demo and Lessons Learned
content:
5.11.1 Demo Live bot: @askfirst_ai2_test_bot on Telegram, running on exactly the environment built in this workshop. Send /start, tap consent, then forward a suspicious message or screenshot. Result screenshots: text message and screenshot in 5.6. Demo video: Minh will add the link (screen recording: sending a text message, sending an image, viewing logs in CloudWatch).
The demo script I use, with a place to verify each step on AWS:
Step On Telegram Cross-check on AWS 1 Send a fake police message demanding a transfer to a “safe account” worker log: ai_invoke op=analyze ... outcome=ok; a new CHECK# appears in the DynamoDB table 2 Send the exact same message again ai log: "cache_hit": true, near-instant reply 3 Send a screenshot of a fake bank SMS containing a link The ai log shows a longer duration (OCR); the result names the fake domain correctly 4 Send a greeting Goes through the fast path, no Bedrock call 5.11.2 Lessons learned 1. Deploy each component first, then connect them. I followed the order S3 → DynamoDB → SSM + Telegram image download → ai Lambda → test-invoke with sample requests → connect to the backend stack. Each step had pass criteria and a negative test (wrong SHA-256 file, wrong file_id, wrong token). When the full pipeline got stuck at “⏳”, I knew right away the AI part was not at fault because it had been tested separately, and found the bug in the contract between webhook and worker: webhook pushed the raw message into SQS, while worker expected an AnalyzeJob. This bug only surfaced when running on real AWS, because each side’s tests were green.
2. Choose memory from a table of measurements. Lambda limits the INIT phase to 10 seconds. At 1769 MB, preloading the models made INIT hit the limit; Lambda cut INIT short and reran it during the first invocation, and the first message took 35 seconds. Three cold starts at three memory settings (section 5.7.2) were enough to choose 3008 MB. The number to keep watching is maxInitMs (9.55 seconds over the last 7 days): every new model preloaded during INIT pushes it closer to the limit.
3. Quantization must be tested on the exact CPU it will run on. The int8 version of VietOCR correctly read 82% of words with diacritics on a laptop, but only 49% on Lambda x86_64. The fp32 version produced identical results on the laptop and on Lambda across all 66 images. Since then, I rerun every model change on a temporary Lambda function before promoting it to the shared environment, then delete that function.
4. Read OCR symptoms correctly. The original OCR model was missing 88 Vietnamese characters (ả ạ ấ ộ ữ…), so it dropped whole vowels: “chuyển tiền” (“transfer money”) became “chuyn tin”. Stripping all diacritics from the reference text and running the rule set had no effect, but losing letters caused 15/33 rule signals to be missed. The fix was to have VietOCR re-read only the Vietnamese lines and merge word by word: correctly read words with diacritics rose from 37% to 89%, missed signals dropped to 6/33, and URLs and phone numbers stayed intact.
5. Test failures by breaking things on purpose. Setting the reserved concurrency of ai to 0 is the cheapest way to simulate the AI part going down. The first attempt showed the user receiving two “busy” messages, and another message could be mistakenly edited into “busy”. No local test caught either of these bugs.
6. An alarm with no recipient might as well not exist. The DLQ alarm transitioned to ALARM at the right time, but AlarmActions was empty, so nobody knew. Now the alarm sends email through SNS, and I test it with set-alarm-state instead of waiting for a real failure.
7. Secrets leak through unexpected places. The bot token once leaked in a terminal screenshot. Since then, the token lives only in SSM SecureString, is read into a shell variable when needed and removed right after, and every screenshot is redacted before being shared.
8. Packaging containers for Lambda has its own pitfalls. The image must preserve the repo’s directory tree because the code locates prompts/ via a relative path; recent Docker versions must build with --provenance=false for Lambda to accept the manifest.
5.11.3 Future improvements Add a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition to the ai role so it can only read/write CACHE# and URL# keys and cannot touch user data. Move the ai Lambda into infra/template.yaml (the AiImageUri parameter) so the whole system deploys with one command, and set RetentionInDays for logs directly in the template. Move some work out of the INIT phase (for example, lazily loading VietOCR on the first image) so maxInitMs keeps a comfortable safety margin below the 10-second limit. Try arm64 (Graviton) Lambda with an embedder that does not depend on the x86 instruction set, since arm64 is cheaper per GB-second. Re-measure OCR accuracy on a fresh, unseen set of images, run exactly once, without tuning the code to the results.
